content: DAPI, also known as 4',6-diamidino-2-phenylindole, is a fluorescent dye that exhibits a strong affinity for DNA. It is widely utilized in fluorescence microscopy due to its ability to bind to DNA. Since DAPI can penetrate intact cell membranes, it is suitable for staining both live and fixed cells. When used in fluorescence microscopy, DAPI is excited by ultraviolet (UV) light. Upon binding to double-stranded DNA, it exhibits an absorption maximum at 358 nm and an emission maximum at 461 nm. The emitted fluorescence is relatively broad and appears as a blue or cyan color. Although DAPI can also bind to RNA, its fluorescence intensity is significantly weaker when bound to RNA. In such cases, the emission spectrum shifts to approximately 500 nm. The blue fluorescence emitted by DAPI is particularly advantageous for researchers who aim to use multiple fluorescent stains within a single sample. However, there is some overlap in fluorescence between DAPI and other green-fluorescent molecules, such as fluorescein and green fluorescent protein (GFP), as well as red-fluorescent stains like Texas Red. This overlap can be mitigated by employing spectral unmixing techniques or capturing images sequentially. In addition to its primary use in labeling cell nuclei, DAPI is frequently employed to detect mycoplasma or viral DNA in cell cultures. Due to its ability to readily enter live cells and bind tightly to DNA, DAPI is considered toxic and mutagenic. Therefore, appropriate precautions must be taken during its handling and disposal. Hoechst stains, which are chemically similar to DAPI, also produce blue fluorescence and are compatible with both live and fixed cell applications.
